steps.do: Locate the row list builder in lib/table/ that renders rows.
Find where table rows are built as TableRow widgets.
Wrap each row in AnimatedOpacity with duration Duration(milliseconds: 180) and opacity starting at 0.0.
Set opacity to 1.0 after Future.delayed with delay Duration(milliseconds: min(index * 30, 300)).
Check that the delay is clamped by writing min(index * 30, 300) in the code, not an unbounded multiply.
Confirm the 180ms fade duration is set in the table files.
Make sure the timer checks mounted before calling setState so it does not run after dispose.

K-004145.example: Row index 4 waits Duration(milliseconds: min(4 * 30, 300)) which is 120ms, then sets opacity to 1.0 with a 180ms AnimatedOpacity. The 180ms grep prints one matching line.
K-004145.check: rg -n 'min\(' prints a line that clamps the delay to 300, the 180ms grep prints one matching line, and rg -n mounted prints a line that guards setState inside the delayed callback.
traps: Using index * 30 with no cap makes the last row in a 200-row table wait 6 seconds.
Skipping the mounted check causes setState called after dispose errors when the user navigates away quickly.
Starting opacity at 1.0 means no fade happens, so the first frame shows full rows and the animation is invisible.

Confirm the normal animated duration of 200ms is still defined in the table files.

Confirm no hard-coded Duration remains outside the helper file.

K-004146.example: tableMotionDuration(context, 200) returns Duration.zero when MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context) is true, and 200ms otherwise. The 200ms grep prints the normal duration line, and the count command prints the number of table widgets that call the helper.
K-004146.check: rg -n 'Duration\(milliseconds' with the motion.dart file excluded prints no lines, the 200ms grep prints one matching line, and rg -c 'tableMotionDuration' prints a count equal to the number of animated table widgets.
traps: Checking MediaQuery.of(context).disableAnimations directly misses the helper's intent, so use MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context) for the flag.
Passing Duration.zero to AnimatedContainer still runs a frame, so the widget should skip the animation entirely where possible.
Leaving one hard-coded Duration in a single row widget breaks reduced motion for that part of the table.

traps: Using px for font sizes instead of rem, which breaks user zoom and browser text-size settings.
Defining tokens inside a component selector instead of :root, so other components cannot reuse them.
Forgetting that the tokens stylesheet must load before the component stylesheet.

steps.do: Define the color tokens in styles/tokens.css: --color-text-title #1a1a1a and --color-surface #ffffff.

Using a light gray such as #999 on white, which falls well below 4.5:1.
Hardcoding hex values in the component instead of referencing the color token.

Create tests/table-responsive.spec.ts that visits /users at widths 320, 768 and 1280 pixels and asserts document.documentElement.scrollWidth equals window.innerWidth at each width.
Run only that spec file so the result is fast and isolated.
If any width fails, rerun the same file with the list reporter to see which width and scrollWidth value differed.

K-004210.example: At width 320 the page scrollWidth is 320 and innerWidth is 320, so the assertion passes and the table scrolls inside .table-wrap with overflow-x: auto. The 1280 case is checked the same way and must also report equal values.
K-004210.check: The output ends with '3 passed' and contains no 'Expected' lines; a failure prints the width and the mismatched scrollWidth.
traps: Checking only desktop width misses the phone overflow that breaks the layout.
Asserting the table element width instead of the document width hides a page-level horizontal scrollbar.
Vitest with jsdom cannot measure layout, so scrollWidth reads 0 there and proves nothing.

steps.do: Create the layout test folder for viewport checks.
Write a Playwright test that sets the viewport to 375 by 667 and reads the boundingBox of every .sort-btn in the table header.
Run that test to get the measured heights and widths of each button.
Confirm every sort button reports at least 44 pixels in height and width, and if one is smaller set min-height: 44px and min-width: 44px on .sort-btn in DataTable.vue.
Rerun the same test after the CSS change to confirm the new sizes.

K-004211.example: The 'Sort by name' button at 375 pixels measures 28 by 24 before the fix and 44 by 44 after adding min-height and min-width. The test asserts both values are at least 44 for every sort button.
K-004211.check: Playwright prints '1 passed' and the logged boundingBox height and width are 44 or more for every .sort-btn.
traps: Measuring at desktop width misses the phone size where the buttons shrink to a smaller box.
Using the 24px WCAG 2.2 AA minimum instead of the 44px target stated in this card lets small buttons pass.
Adding padding without min-height or min-width can leave the hit area under 44px.

steps.do: Build the app so axe scans the production CSS rather than dev-only styles.
Serve the built app on a fixed port in a separate terminal and keep it running.
Run axe against the users table page limited to the color-contrast rule and exit with a failure code on violations.
For each reported selector such as .sticky-th, raise the text color until its ratio is at least 4.5:1 against its background, and write down the new value.
Rerun the same axe command to confirm zero violations.

K-004212.example: The sticky header text #8a8a8a on #ffffff measures 3.5:1 and fails, so axe reports the selector .sticky-th. Changing the text to #595959 measures 7.0:1 and passes on the rerun.
K-004212.check: The final axe run lists no violations and exits with code 0.
traps: Scanning the Vite dev server can miss styles that exist only in the production build.
Applying the 3:1 large-text threshold to normal-size table header text lets failing colors pass.
Fixing only the hover or focus color leaves the default header state failing.

steps.do: Create the component spec file next to DataTable.vue.
In a beforeEach block, stub window.matchMedia to report a match for the query (max-width: 639px) and restore the original in afterEach.
Mount DataTable with @vue/test-utils using a four-row fixture and assert that no tr elements render in card mode while four .card-row elements do.
Run that spec file with Vitest.
Add a desktop test that stubs matchMedia to return no match and rerun only that test to confirm the table renders.

K-004213.example: With the stub matching '(max-width: 639px)', wrapper.findAll('tr').length is 0 and wrapper.findAll('.card-row').length is 4 for the four-row fixture. The desktop test expects the opposite counts.
K-004213.check: Vitest prints 'Tests 2 passed' and the .card-row count equals the fixture row count.
traps: jsdom has no real layout, so this test checks the Vue branch and not pixel widths.
Forgetting to restore matchMedia lets one test's width leak into the next test.
Matching against wrapper.html() strings is fragile; counting elements is more reliable.

steps.do: Create a reports folder for the Lighthouse output.
Run Lighthouse in the mobile form factor against the built users page and write the result as JSON.
Read the cumulative-layout-shift numericValue from the JSON file.
If the value is above 0.1, set fixed column widths on the table and reserve the row height for the skeleton state so rows stop moving after load.
Rerun Lighthouse and the jq read to confirm the new value.

K-004214.example: The mobile CLS for /users reads 0.27 before the fix, caused by a skeleton row that changed height when data arrived. After fixing the row height and column widths the same jq command prints 0.04.
K-004214.check: The jq command prints a number of 0.1 or less.
traps: Running desktop Lighthouse hides shifts that appear only at mobile width.
Lighthouse must scan the running built app, or it scores an error page and reports a misleading CLS.
Reading the performance score instead of the CLS value can hide a bad shift behind a passing total.

steps.do: Install project dependencies so Playwright and Vue resolve correctly.
Write a test that sets the viewport to 360 by 740, sets .table-wrap scrollLeft to 200, and reads the x position of the first th.
Run only the sticky test by name to isolate the check.
If the first column x is not 0 after scrolling, add position: sticky with left: 0 and a solid background to the first th and td cells in DataTable.vue.
Rerun the sticky test to confirm the fix.

K-004215.example: After setting scrollLeft to 200 the first th x is 0 while the fifth column x is negative, showing the first column stayed pinned. The test asserts the first th x equals 0 after the scroll.
K-004215.check: Playwright prints '1 passed' and the logged first th x is 0.
traps: Scrolling the window instead of .table-wrap tests the wrong element and passes falsely.
Setting sticky on the wrapper instead of the th and td cells pins nothing.
Omitting a background on the sticky cells lets scrolled content show through behind the pinned column.

steps.do: Find where the toast background material is applied.
Add an @Environment accessibilityReduceTransparency property to the toast view.
Use the ToastBackground color at full opacity when that property is true, and the material otherwise.
Confirm the reduce transparency property is referenced in the view file.
Measure foreground text against the solid fallback in both schemes and confirm at least 4.5:1 contrast.

K-004216.example: When reduceTransparency is true, the toast fills with ToastBackground at full opacity instead of .ultraThinMaterial. Primary text on that fill must measure at least 4.5:1.
K-004216.check: rg shows the material line guarded by a reduce transparency condition, and the contrast measurement is 4.5:1 or higher in both schemes.
traps: Lowering the material's opacity without a solid base lets the content behind the toast show through.
Skipping the contrast measurement lets light text on a light fallback pass unnoticed.

steps.do: Create the theme file in the toast module.
Define a ToastTheme struct with background, foreground, and border Color properties.
Declare a private EnvironmentKey with a static defaultValue set to ToastTheme.default.
Confirm the file declares the environment key.
Confirm no literal Color(red:green:blue:) values remain in the theme file.
Check that the default theme's white foreground on the dark background meets 4.5:1 WCAG contrast.

K-004217.example: ToastTheme.default uses Color('ToastBackground', bundle: .module) for its background. Callers apply the theme with .environment on the ToastHost view using the toastTheme key path.
K-004217.check: grep -n prints one EnvironmentKey line, grep -c prints 0, and the contrast command prints a ratio of at least 4.5.
traps: Forgetting defaultValue makes the key fail for views outside the host.
Hard-coding Color(red:green:blue:) inside the theme defeats dark mode because it never changes with appearance.

steps.do: Find the toast view file to add previews to.
Add a #Preview block that applies .preferredColorScheme(.light) to ToastView.
Add a second #Preview block that applies .preferredColorScheme(.dark) to ToastView.
Count the preview blocks to confirm both schemes exist.
Confirm the view reads colorScheme from the environment.
Check that the toast text on the dark preview background meets 4.5:1 WCAG contrast.

K-004218.example: The light preview applies .preferredColorScheme(.light) and the dark preview applies .preferredColorScheme(.dark), each wrapping ToastView(message: 'Saved').
K-004218.check: grep -c prints 2, grep -n shows an @Environment line for colorScheme, and the contrast command prints a ratio of at least 4.5.
traps: Previewing only in light mode hides dark contrast failures.
Setting preferredColorScheme on a parent container instead of each preview can make both previews show the same scheme.

steps.do: Find every validator return statement to reuse existing wording and avoid conflicting messages.
Count the lines in the validators file to get a baseline size for the plan.
Plan each error string as a complete sentence of at most 80 characters that names the field and the fix.
Plan the error text to use Theme.of(context).colorScheme.error on colorScheme.surface, and check that the ratio is at least 4.5:1.
Plan Semantics with liveRegion set to true on the empty-state headline so screen readers announce it when it appears.

K-004219.example: The email validator in lib/core/validators.dart returns Enter an email like name@example.com, which is 33 characters and under the 80-character cap. The error text uses colorScheme.error on colorScheme.surface, and the plan records a 4.5:1 contrast check for it.
K-004219.check: rg -n 'return' lib/core/validators.dart prints one message per validator with no empty string, and wc -l reports the line count the plan recorded.
traps: Small models write vague errors like Invalid that do not say how to fix the field.
Do not use color alone to show an error because users with color blindness will miss it.
The 4.5:1 ratio is for body text, so check it with a contrast tool, not by eye.

steps.do: Find every DropdownButtonFormField and see which ones can receive an empty items list at runtime.
Find the items sources so you can see which lists are built from data that may be empty.
Check for an existing EmptyState widget to reuse instead of creating a second one.
Plan that when the item list length is 0 the field shows an icon, one headline line and a FilledButton that opens the add flow, and the validator returns Choose a payment method as the error text.
Plan the FilledButton to be at least 48 logical pixels tall so it meets the Material minimum tap target.

K-004220.example: lib/features/billing/payment_method_field.dart builds a DropdownButtonFormField from a repository that can return an empty list. The plan replaces the menu with a 48-logical-pixel FilledButton labeled Add payment method and keeps the validator returning Choose a payment method when no value is set.
K-004220.check: rg -n DropdownButtonFormField lib prints each file and line, the plan names every one that has an empty-list branch, and the EmptyState search shows whether a reusable empty-state widget already exists.
traps: Small models add a new EmptyState class when the search already finds one.
Do not make the validator return null for an empty list because that passes the form silently.
The validator alone cannot fix a dropdown with zero items, so the empty-state branch is required.

steps.do: Find the existing test files to see the project's baseline of widget tests.
Check for an existing test that uses tester.enterText so the new test can reuse its pattern.
Count the testWidgets cases already in the test folder to avoid duplicating them. Record the printed total as the baseline number.
Write the planned list: one testWidgets case for an empty list showing EmptyState, one for submit with an empty field showing the error text, and one for a valid submit calling onSubmit exactly once.
After the test file is written, count its testWidgets cases. The number must be exactly 3, and the suite total must be the baseline from the earlier count plus 3.

K-004221.example: test/widgets/empty_state_test.dart plans three testWidgets cases, and rg -c testWidgets test returns 9 for the existing suite, so the new file brings the total to 12. The submit case uses tester.enterText on the email field and taps the FilledButton, and the plan sets a 30-second limit for the file.
K-004221.check: rg -c testWidgets test prints the existing count, and the planned list in the plan has exactly as many new cases as the number written.
traps: Small models plan a test that only checks the widget renders and skip the validation branch.
Do not skip the empty-list case, since it is the one most likely to break.
A planned test is not a passing test, so verification has to come from running the Flutter test command.

steps.do: Confirm the Vue accessibility lint plugin is installed in node_modules.
Run ESLint on the menu component file and expect no warnings.
Count the role attributes declared in the menu template.

K-004222.example: The file src/components/AppMenu.vue has a trigger button with only an icon, so ESLint reports vuejs-accessibility/control-has-associated-label. After adding visible text or an aria-label attribute, npx eslint exits with code 0 and grep -c role= returns at least 3.
K-004222.check: npx eslint prints nothing and exits 0, and grep -c role= prints a number of 3 or more; any line containing vuejs-accessibility means failure.
traps: Small models often lint the wrong path or forget to add the plugin to the eslint config.
A clean lint result does not prove keyboard support, so the card's other steps are still required.

steps.do: Confirm the menu axe spec file exists under src.
Run only the axe spec for the menu component.
List the number of axe violations the spec expects to be zero.

K-004223.example: The spec mounts AppMenu with @vue/test-utils mount, then calls await axe(wrapper.html()) and expects toHaveNoViolations. After the fix, npx vitest run reports 1 passed and zero violations.
K-004223.check: npx vitest run prints a line like Tests 1 passed (1) and no axe violation lists; grep -c prints 1 or more.
traps: Small models forget to await wrapper.vm.$nextTick before running axe, so open-state markup is missing.
jsdom cannot measure color contrast, so do not claim contrast passed from this card.

steps.do: Confirm the keyboard spec file references the ArrowDown key.
Run the Playwright keyboard spec for the menu.
Check that the spec presses Escape to close the menu.

K-004224.example: The spec opens the menu with Enter, presses ArrowDown twice, and expects focus on the third menuitem. The Vue component handles @keydown.down and @keydown.esc, so the run prints 1 passed.
K-004224.check: grep counts are 1 or more each, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with no failed tests.
traps: Small models write tests that click instead of pressing keys, which misses the keyboard path.
Playwright needs the dev server running, so start it before running the spec.

steps.do: Confirm the component binds aria-expanded to the open state.
Run the focus-return unit test in Vitest.
steps.cmd: npx vitest run src/components/AppMenu.spec.ts -t focus returns to trigger

steps.do: Count the ref calls that store the trigger element for focus restore.

K-004225.example: The component uses ref triggerRef on the button and calls triggerRef.value.focus() inside closeMenu, and the test asserts document.activeElement equals the button. The run prints Tests 1 passed.
K-004225.check: grep -n shows a line containing :aria-expanded, grep -c triggerRef returns 2 or more, and vitest prints 1 passed.
traps: Small models use document.getElementById in Vue code instead of a template ref, which breaks inside components.
The focus call must run after the DOM update, so wrap it in nextTick when needed.

steps.do: Confirm the component style block sets a 44px minimum height on menu items.
Run the Playwright target-size spec that measures each menuitem bounding box.
Confirm the spec compares the measured height against 44px.

K-004226.example: The style block sets min-height: 44px on .menu-item, and the spec reads boundingBox().height for each item and expects at least 44. The run prints 1 passed with every item at 44px or taller.
K-004226.check: grep -n prints a line containing min-height: 44px, grep -c prints 1 or more, and Playwright reports 1 passed.
traps: Small models set 44px on a wrapper but not on the clickable menuitem, so the real target stays small.
Padding that is smaller than 44px total does not count, so measure the rendered box.

steps.do: List the color declarations in the menu component to find the text and background pair.
Run the Playwright contrast spec that runs axe color-contrast on the open menu.
Confirm the spec runs the color-contrast rule from axe.

K-004227.example: The menu text is #595959 on #ffffff, which is 7:1, and the spec opens the menu before running axe with the color-contrast rule enabled. The run prints 1 passed with zero color-contrast violations.
K-004227.check: grep -n shows the color values, grep -c returns 1 or more, and Playwright prints 1 passed with no color-contrast violation.
traps: Small models check the default color but skip hover, focus, and disabled item states, which often fall below 4.5:1.
Use contrast ratios of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, and check each state.

steps.do: Create the components folder if it does not exist.
Create the AppButton.vue file that will hold the component.
In script setup, declare size as a union of sm, md, and lg using withDefaults with md as the default.
In a scoped style block, set min-height 2rem and font-size 1rem on the base button class.
Inside an @media (pointer: coarse) block, set min-height 44px and min-width 44px on the button.
Lint the component with the Vue rules from eslint.
Confirm the 44px rule appears in the component source.

K-004228.example: The base rule uses min-height 2rem and the coarse media block raises it to 44px. The grep command prints one matching line with the AppButton.vue path and its line number.
K-004228.check: eslint exits with no output, and grep prints one line that contains min-height: 44px inside src/components/AppButton.vue.
traps: Setting only height and forgetting min-height lets text grow the box past 44px.
Placing the media query outside the scoped style block means it is not compiled into the component.
Using 44px on a fine pointer forces large buttons on mouse users.

steps.do: Find the line where the scoped style block starts in the button component.
Set width auto as the default for the button class.
Add a @media (max-width: 40rem) rule that sets width 100% and display block on the button class.
Build the app to confirm the media query compiles without errors.
Run the Playwright test that sets a 375px by 667px viewport and checks the button width.

K-004229.example: At a 375px viewport with 16px page padding on each side, the button measures 343px wide. At 1024px it shrinks back to its content width because 40rem equals 640px at the default root size.
K-004229.check: The grep prints a line number for the style block, the vite build exits 0, and Playwright prints 1 passed with the measured width of 343px.
traps: Using min-width in place of max-width reverses the breakpoint logic.
Forgetting display block leaves the button inline so width has no effect.
Testing at only one viewport misses the breakpoint edge at 640px.

steps.do: Confirm the build target supports container queries by reading the target line in the Vite config.
Add container-type inline-size and container-name card to the parent wrapper style.
Add an @container card (max-width: 20rem) rule that sets the button font-size to 0.875rem.
Mount the button in a 240px wide sidebar and in a 600px wide panel on a test page.
Run the component test that measures the font size at both widths.

K-004230.example: The sidebar at 240px gets 0.875rem (14px) label text and the panel at 600px keeps 1rem (16px). The @container rule matches the card width, not the window width.
K-004230.check: vitest prints Test Files 1 passed, the sidebar font size is 14px, and the panel font size is 16px.
traps: Setting container-type on the button itself, which cannot query its own size.
Using @media instead of @container, which reacts to the window and not the parent card.
Writing a container query without the container-name that the rule refers to.

steps.do: Create the composables folder if it does not exist.
Create the useMediaQuery.ts file that exports a ref updated from window.matchMedia.
Inside the composable, read matchMedia in onMounted, register a change listener, and remove it in onBeforeUnmount.
Use the composable in AppButton.vue to hide the text label when the query matches.
Run the TypeScript check on the project.
Run the unit test that sets the matchMedia mock to 375px and asserts the label is hidden.

K-004231.example: useMediaQuery('(max-width: 40rem)') returns a ref that is true at 375px. The button renders the label span only when isNarrow is false.
K-004231.check: tsc exits 0 with no output, and vitest prints 1 passed with the assertion that isNarrow.value equals true at 375px.
traps: Forgetting to remove the listener leaks memory on every unmount.
Reading window.matchMedia outside onMounted breaks server-side rendering because window does not exist there.
Starting the ref with the wrong initial value makes the first render disagree with the viewport.

steps.do: Declare the size prop with withDefaults and a union type of sm, md, and lg.
Add a sizes map where sm uses 2.25rem height, md uses 2.75rem height, and lg uses 3rem height.
Bind a computed style object with :style that applies the height and padding for the chosen size.
Lint the component with the Vue plugin rules.
Count the height declarations in the component to confirm there are three size tokens.

K-004232.example: The md size uses 2.75rem, which is 44px at a 16px root size. The grep count prints 3 and eslint prints nothing.
K-004232.check: eslint exits 0 with no output, and grep -c prints 3.
traps: Using px values makes the button ignore the user's root font size setting.
Setting sm below 2.75rem height may fail the 44px touch target on touch screens.
Skipping the union type lets an invalid size string reach the component at runtime.

steps.do: Set font-size with clamp using 0.875rem as the minimum, 2.5vw as the preferred value, and 1rem as the maximum.
Set white-space nowrap, overflow hidden, and text-overflow ellipsis on the label span.
Set max-width 100% and min-width 0 on the button so flex parents can shrink it.
Build the Vite bundle to confirm the scoped styles compile.
Run the Playwright check that measures the button width at a 320px viewport.

K-004233.example: font-size clamp(0.875rem, 2.5vw, 1rem) gives 14px at 320px wide and 16px at 640px wide or more. A 320px viewport minus 32px of padding leaves a button no wider than 288px.
K-004233.check: vite build exits 0, and Playwright prints 1 passed with the button width at most 288px at a 320px viewport.
traps: Forgetting min-width 0 means flex children never shrink below their content width.
Applying text-overflow ellipsis to the button when only the label span needs it.
Using px for the clamp bounds means the text no longer scales with the user's root font size.

steps.do: Confirm the label stays in the view tree and only its opacity changes while loading.
Confirm a fixed minimum width of 120pt is set on the label container.
Count the ProgressView uses to confirm a single spinner per button.

K-004234.example: LoadingButton.swift applies .frame(minWidth: 120) and .opacity(isLoading ? 0 : 1) to the Text label, and overlays one ProgressView. The count command prints 1 for that file.
K-004234.check: The minWidth grep prints one match with the value 120; the opacity grep prints one match; the ProgressView count is 1 per button file.
traps: Removing the Text from the view tree when loading makes the button shrink and shift neighbors.
Using a ProgressView without a fixed frame lets the button resize in Dynamic Type.
Adding a second spinner inside the label duplicates the animation.

steps.do: Confirm the button frame sets a minimum height of 44 points.
Confirm the disabled foreground color keeps at least 4.5:1 contrast against the background.
Confirm the ProgressView is not larger than the label, so the frame does not grow.

K-004235.example: LoadingButton.swift uses .frame(minHeight: 44) and .controlSize(.regular) so the ProgressView stays within the 44pt frame. A disabled gray of #767676 on white gives a 4.54:1 ratio, which passes.
K-004235.check: The minHeight grep prints a match with 44; the contrast check reports 4.5:1 or higher; the controlSize match confirms no enlarged spinner.
traps: Reducing padding while loading can drop the tap target below 44pt.
Using a light gray disabled color on white can fall under 4.5:1 contrast.
Using .controlSize(.large) on the spinner can push the button past its intended height.

steps.do: Confirm the button sets an accessibility value that changes during loading.
Confirm the loading value is the word Loading and it is set only when isLoading is true.
Confirm the test file states the 200ms latency bound for the VoiceOver announcement.

K-004236.example: SubmitButton.swift sets .accessibilityValue(isLoading ? "Loading" : "") on the Button. The first rg output shows that line at line 21, and the third rg output shows a 200ms bound in the test file.
K-004236.check: The first rg prints one line with accessibilityValue set to a conditional on isLoading; the third rg prints a line containing the number 200 that bounds the announcement at 200ms.
traps: A spinner alone is silent to VoiceOver, so the state must be exposed as text.
Setting the accessibilityLabel to Loading replaces the button name, which hides what the button does.
Posting a notification for every frame of the spinner floods the user with announcements.

steps.do: Find the await block that wraps the modal's loading state.
Run the Svelte checker to catch template errors in the modal.
Run the loading Playwright test, which delays the API response by 2000 ms.
Confirm the spec asserts exactly one element with role status while the request is pending.

K-004237.example: The spec routes /api/report with a 2000 ms delay, clicks the Open report button, and expects getByRole('status') to have count 1 within 200 ms. After the response resolves, the same locator must have count 0.
K-004237.check: The Playwright output ends with '1 passed' and grep prints at least one line containing {#await inside src/lib.
traps: Small models place the await block outside the <dialog>, so the spinner renders before showModal() runs. Keep the await inside the dialog element.
Do not replace the assertion with a fixed sleep; use the role locator so the test waits on the real state.
Do not count the spinner by class name; assert on role status.

steps.do: Check that the dialog element sets aria-busy from its loading state variable.
Start the dev server in the background on port 5173 so the audit can reach the modal.
Run axe against the page with the modal open, limited to WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 A and AA rules.
Run the focus trap test that tabs 10 times during loading and records the focused element.

K-004238.example: The dialog sets aria-busy={loading} and the focus test presses Tab 10 times while the 2000 ms request is pending. Every focused element must have a closest dialog ancestor.
K-004238.check: grep prints an aria-busy line, axe exits with status 0 and reports no violations, and the Playwright output ends with '1 passed'.
traps: Small models set aria-busy on the wrapper div instead of the element that holds the busy content. Put it on the element whose content is loading.
Do not skip the focus test because axe passed; axe does not check focus order.
Do not run npm run dev without a port flag, or the audit URL may point at the wrong server.

steps.do: Find the disabled binding on the submit button in the modal component.
Run the Playwright test that clicks submit twice during a 2000 ms request and counts POST calls.
Confirm the spec asserts the submit button has the disabled attribute while loading and that the POST count is 1.

K-004239.example: The spec clicks the Send button at 0 ms and again at 500 ms, then expects the button to have disabled and the mocked POST count to equal 1. After the response, the button must be enabled again.
K-004239.check: The Playwright output ends with '1 passed' and the grep output includes a line with disabled={loading} or similar.
traps: Small models disable the button with a CSS class only, which does not block clicks. Use the disabled attribute.
Do not forget to re-enable the button in the success and error paths; the test must also check that.
Count network requests, not clicks, to prove only one submit happened.

steps.do: Run axe with the color-contrast rule against the modal in its loading state.
Run the Playwright test that measures the cancel button bounding box height.
Confirm the spec expects the cancel button height to be at least 44 px and the spinner text contrast to be at least 4.5:1.

K-004240.example: The cancel button has min-height: 44px in the Modal.svelte style block, and the spinner label #595959 on #ffffff measures 7.0:1. The size test asserts boundingBox().height >= 44.
K-004240.check: axe exits with status 0 with no color-contrast violations, and the Playwright output ends with '1 passed'.
traps: Small models compute contrast from memory and get it wrong. Let axe measure it instead of guessing.
A min-height of 1rem is far below the 44px target; use 44px for touch targets.
Do not test contrast on the open state only; the loading state has different colors.

steps.do: Find where the loading flag is set to true before the fetch starts.
Run the Playwright test that clicks open and expects the status element to be visible within 200 ms.
Confirm the spec uses toBeVisible with a timeout of 200 and not a longer default.

K-004241.example: The spec clicks the Open button and calls expect(page.getByRole('status')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 200 }) while the mocked request holds for 2000 ms. The test fails if the spinner takes longer than 200 ms.
K-004241.check: grep shows the loading = true assignment, and the Playwright output ends with '1 passed'.
traps: Small models set loading to true after await fetch, so the spinner appears only after the response. Set it before the fetch.
The default expect timeout is 5000 ms, which hides slow spinners. Set the timeout to 200.
Do not use Date.now() in the test; the Playwright assertion already waits.

steps.do: Find the catch branch of the await block in the modal.
Run the Playwright test that aborts the API route and checks the spinner and error text.
Run the Svelte checker to confirm the catch block types correctly.
Confirm the spec expects getByRole status to have count 0 and an alert element to be visible after the abort.

K-004242.example: The spec calls route.abort() on /api/report, then expects getByRole('status') to have count 0 and getByRole('alert') to contain 'Could not load report'. The modal must still be open with the close button enabled.
K-004242.check: grep prints a {:catch line, svelte-check reports 0 errors, and the Playwright output ends with '1 passed'.
traps: Small models leave loading as true in the catch branch, so the spinner never goes away. Reset the flag in both branches.
